source.title: Normalization Layers Are All That Sharpness-Aware Minimization Needs
source.authors: Maximilian Mueller; Tiffany J. Vlaar; D. Rolnick; Matthias Hein

record.tranche_reason: The study measures adaptive sharpness and test accuracy, and reports that SAM-ON models can be sharper yet perform better. This qualifies the claim that sharpness tracks generalization.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own sharpness and test-accuracy measurements. Other findings about SAM-ON, sparse perturbations, robustness, and parameter distributions do not bear on the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures magnitude-scaled sharpness and held-out accuracy within two convolutional architectures, finding sharper SAM-ON models with better accuracy. Appendix B.10 states that CIFAR training error is close to zero, making test error an approximate generalization-gap measure here. Additional batch-size and dropout experiments bear on V5 and V6, although their effects cannot be determined from the supplied figure text.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate: SAM-ON can improve generalization while losing some of SAM-all's sharpness reduction, so reduced sharpness alone does not explain SAM's benefits. The authors also emphasize the special role of normalization parameters rather than perturbation sparsity alone.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a parameter-restricted SAM perturbation (normalization-layer affine parameters only) with SAM applied to all parameters; sharpness is estimated using 20-step AutoPGD and a one-step measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The comparison varies architecture (WRN-28, ResNeXt), training method (SAM or ASAM variants), and sharpness radius.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM-ON often improves accuracy, robustness and computational cost compared with SAM-all.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Restricting SAM perturbations to normalization parameters can improve its performance and efficiency.

fits_no_version.finding: Smaller sharpness subbatches m improve performance within a fixed optimizer batch size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The subbatch size used for SAM's adversarial ascent affects held-out performance.

record.problems: The study reports test accuracy rather than the train–test gap for these comparisons. Its sharpness analysis covers selected architectures and training methods; it does not evaluate the version's comparison against norm- and margin-based measures.
record.rows_left_out: Table 6 and Table 18 also report one-step sharpness values; these were omitted because the study's description emphasizes the 20-step measure as its sharpness comparison. Table 19 reports additional, non-logit-normalized sharpness definitions, which do not match V7's stated measure.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting compared with natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on matched architectures and tasks under comparable tuning.
Language models, longer-training remedies, and identification of a workload-dependent batch-size threshold.
Very small training sets, dropout throughout classifiers, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.

Ranking against norm- and margin-based measures; the original CIFAR-10/SVHN setting without augmentation; directly documented matching of training losses. The study uses CIFAR-100 with augmentation and reports near-zero training error rather than matched training loss.
Removing highly memorized examples and comparing with equally sized random removals.

missing.what: Additional 20-step adaptive-sharpness radii, not declared omitted: WRN-28 at 0.005 and 0.007 and ResNeXt at 0.003 and 0.005. Every ON/all comparison retains the reversed sharpness–accuracy ordering.

Fixed-epoch batch-size comparison for WRN-28 on CIFAR-100, with batches 128, 256 and 512 and varying sharpness subbatch m. Extract accuracy comparisons at matched m to isolate optimizer batch size. The supplied figure text does not reveal the curve values, so no V5 verdict is justified.

Dropout-rate sweep applied only to normalization parameters or activations in WRN-28 on CIFAR-100. Record held-out accuracy against zero dropout for each implementation. The prose only establishes that these methods do not match SAM-ON; it does not establish their effect versus zero dropout.

record.verdict_notes: The record overlooks Appendix B.10's explicit near-zero training-error statement. Its blanket challenges verdict is too broad: V7 already allows failed sharpness comparisons, and these experiments extend beyond its stated dataset and augmentation conditions. Non-logit-normalized magnitude-aware measures can also bear on V7; their omission was declared, so they are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Network width beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets.

The study does not test whether the measure ranks generalization gaps better than norm- and margin-based measures, or compare networks trained to similarly low training loss across the broader set of conditions described in the version.

relation.reason: The study directly compares magnitude-aware sharpness and held-out performance within fixed convolutional architectures; Appendix B.10 justifies approximating the generalization gap by test error.

tranche.reason: Tables 6 and 18 and Section 5.2 report sharper normalization-only models with better held-out accuracy, requiring qualification of the sharpness–generalization relationship.

source_check.notes: Sharpness is logit-normalized adaptive loss increase, evaluated on 2048 training examples with m=128; near-zero training error is asserted qualitatively. The authors' conclusion is accurate; these comparisons do not test V7's ranking against norm- or margin-based measures.
